set.plain: Five people from a court-supervised treatment programme were scanned twice. After a year or more without meth, their dopamine transporter levels had risen by about a sixth to a fifth. No one who doesn't use meth was scanned twice for comparison, so normal differences between scans can't be ruled out, though one review thinks they are unlikely to explain the rise. A group scanned after many months without meth, which included these five, was not clearly different from people who don't use. But the groups were too small to rule out a large difference. Three studies found no link between how long people had gone without meth and their transporter levels. In another small study, levels rose over two weeks, but the first scan was taken while meth still showed up in urine tests. A later follow-up by the same research group has not yet been read. Five people is too few to know how typical this is, and those who stayed abstinent had higher levels to begin with.
set.grade.domains.inconsistency.note: Three cross-sectional analyses (one from the same programme) found no relation between time since last use and transporter levels, whereas two small follow-ups (this one and a SPECT study) found a rise.

set.plain: Brain scans taken about a week after stopping showed some regions with less grey matter (differences of up to about 11% in one study) in people dependent on meth. Other studies, of people who had stopped for 3–4 months on average or were still using, found some regions larger, including parts of the same deep brain structures. Most people who use meth also smoke tobacco, and in the study that checked, smokers who don't use meth showed some of the same differences. People who used meth also had less schooling and more symptoms of depression. In one study, grey matter grew in several regions over the first month without meth, though only by a lenient statistical standard. An early finding of a smaller memory region (the hippocampus) was not repeated by the same lab.
